question: Europe has experienced four consecutive record-breaking heatwaves over the summer of 2026. Preliminary data indicates at least 35 000 excess deaths, although the figures available cover only around half the continent and do not yet include all the data for August. The data demonstrates that extreme heat is a growing threat to public health.

The Commission is currently preparing the upcoming European climate resilience and risk management framework, which should strengthen the Union’s capacity to anticipate and manage growing climate risks. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission incorporate the rising death rate linked to extreme heat into the future European climate resilience and risk management framework?
Will the framework contain specific measures to reduce exposure and vulnerability to heat and especially to protect the most vulnerable individuals and groups?
How will the Commission ensure that the future framework establishes an effective European response to the health risks posed by extreme heat, beyond new planning and assessment obligations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) The forthcoming EU Framework for Climate Resilience1 will propose a common global warming reference trajectory, to help determine expected levels of heat stress across Europe and that public authorities must prepare for.

The Commission is also exploring how to incorporate metrics for measuring the effects of the new framework, including possibly effects on heat-related mortality. Extreme heat will be one of the climate impacts to be addressed under the upcoming Climate Resilience Framework. In addition, the Health Security Committee, published in July, an opinion on addressing the health impacts of heatwaves and extreme heat2.

In her 2026 State of the Union Address, the President of the Commission announced that the Commission will soon present a European Heatwave Plan. It will address the need for better early warning systems and better health preparedness, urban adaptation and cooling, reducing environmental vulnerabilities, and supporting the most vulnerable.

The new Climate Resilience Framework will set the basis for systematic and anticipatory climate risk management and ensure that the EU and Member States act more in concert. A core element, the proposed European Climate Resilience Law, will aim to make public policy and action for climate preparedness and resilience simpler, clearer, easier to understand and implement.
This will also empower and encourage individuals and businesses to address climate risks by providing information, digital tools, ideas and solutions.
